Title: I built YouTubeRAG because n8n kept failing
Body:
I built YouTubeRAG because n8n kept failing me. 90 minutes to build. Infinitely more reliable. Here's how it works:

1/ The Problem — n8n + RapidAPI workflow for YouTube transcripts. Broke constantly. Rate limits. API changes. Random failures. I was spending more time fixing automation than it saved.

2/ The Solution: Build My Own — FastAPI microservice on port 3011. Components: youtube-transcript-api for extraction, SpaCy for semantic chunking, OpenAI for embeddings, ChromaDB for vector storage.

3/ The Pipeline — Input: YouTube video/playlist URL. Steps: Extract transcripts → Chunk into semantic segments → Generate embeddings → Store in vector DB → Ready for queries. 17 videos → 103 chunks → searchable knowledge base.

4/ The Chunking Strategy — Not fixed-size. Semantic. Using SpaCy to detect topic boundaries. Preserving time markers for navigation. Result: Chunks that make sense, not arbitrary splits.

5/ The Query Interface — Natural language in → relevant chunks out. 'What's the best scraping technique?' → Top 3 relevant segments → Source video + timestamp → Full context preserved.

6/ The Architecture Win — Made it an API. Not siloed to one project. Now ANY project can ingest videos, query the knowledge base, get cited answers. Infrastructure that compounds.

7/ Time Comparison — Manual note-taking: 40 minutes per video. YouTubeRAG query: 30 seconds. Built once. Use forever. That's the power of owning your automation.

Title: Your RAG system is probably broken
Body:
Your RAG system is probably broken. And you don't know it because you're not measuring the right things. Here's what I learned building YouTubeRAG:

1/ The Common Mistakes — Fixed-size chunks (breaks mid-thought), pure vector search (misses exact matches), no source attribution (can't verify), giant context windows (slow, expensive). Most RAG tutorials teach these.

2/ Chunking Strategy Matters — Don't split on character count. Use semantic boundaries: topic changes, speaker transitions, natural pauses. SpaCy can detect these automatically.

3/ Hybrid Search Wins — Vector search: 'What's the concept?' Keyword search: 'Where's the exact term?' Use both. My YouTubeRAG combines semantic + keyword. Retrieval quality: dramatically better.

4/ Metadata is Crucial — Store with each chunk: source document, timestamp/position, original context, confidence score. You'll need these for verification and navigation.

5/ Context Window Management — Don't stuff everything in. Retrieve relevant chunks → rerank → take top K. Less context = faster, cheaper, often more accurate.

6/ Test Your Retrieval — Before connecting to an LLM: query the vector DB directly, check if right chunks return, measure precision/recall. Bad retrieval + good LLM = garbage output.

7/ The Meta-Lesson — RAG isn't about the model. It's about how you chunk, how you embed, how you retrieve. Fix the pipeline. Then worry about the model.

Title: How I debug automation failures systematically
Body:
How I debug automation failures systematically. My scheduler broke for 3 days. Here's how I fixed it:

1/ The Symptom — 60 agents weren't running. No errors in logs. Scheduler started fine. Silent failure. The worst kind.

2/ Step 1: Verify the Basics — Is the script executable? Are paths correct? Are dependencies installed? Are env vars set? Often the fix is embarrassingly simple.

3/ Step 2: Trace the Execution — Add logging at every step: script started, each agent triggered, each agent completed, errors caught. Find where execution stops.

4/ Step 3: Check Environment — Cron/LaunchAgent run in different env than terminal. Different PATH, different working directory, different permissions. Print env vars. Compare to manual run.

5/ The Root Cause — Hardcoded path: /Users/old/path/to/project. Worked until I moved folders. Scheduler tried to access non-existent path. Error was caught and... swallowed. Lesson: Never hardcode paths.

6/ The Fix — Use relative paths, use environment variables, make error handling loud not quiet, add health checks that alert on failure.

7/ The Prevention — Now every agent has verbose logging option, health check endpoint, failure alerts, self-healing restart logic. Silent failures are now impossible.

Title: Simple automation beats complex automation
Body:
Simple automation beats complex automation. Every time. Here's what I learned building 60+ agents:

1/ The Temptation — Build one mega-script that handles all cases, has every feature, covers every edge case. Feels comprehensive. Actually fragile.

2/ The Reality — Complex automation: hard to debug, hard to modify, fails catastrophically, single point of failure. Simple automation: easy to understand, easy to fix, fails gracefully, isolated failures.

3/ My Rule — One agent = one job. Not 'project management agent.' Instead: GitHub sync agent, TODO aggregation agent, Security scoring agent. Composable pieces.

4/ The Coordination Layer — Daily scheduler orchestrates. Agents do the work. Scheduler is simple: call agents in sequence. Agents are simple: do one thing well. Complexity in coordination, not execution.

5/ Error Handling Philosophy — Old: Catch everything, never fail. New: Fail fast, log loudly, alert me. I'd rather know about problems than have them hidden.

6/ The Maintenance Burden — Complex: Hours to understand, minutes to break. Simple: Minutes to understand, seconds to fix. Your future self will thank you.

7/ The Meta-Lesson — Automation should reduce complexity, not add it. If your automation needs automation, you've gone too far. Simple. Reliable. Boring. That's the goal.

Title: How I use Plan Mode effectively

2/ When to Use It — Unfamiliar codebase, multiple approaches possible, changes affect many files, need to understand before acting. Complex tasks need exploration.

3/ The Workflow — Phase 1 Explore: 'Read src/auth and explain how sessions work.' Phase 2 Plan: 'I want to add OAuth. What files need to change?' Phase 3 Implement: [Exit Plan Mode] 'Implement the OAuth flow.'

6/ When NOT to Use It — Simple, obvious tasks. You know the codebase well. Change is isolated to one file. Time-sensitive fix. Planning adds overhead. Skip for trivial work.

7/ The Result — Fewer mistakes. Better implementations. Less wasted effort. Explore → Plan → Execute. That's how complex changes become manageable.

Title: How I manage context in long Claude Code sessions
Body:
How I manage context in long Claude Code sessions. The #1 resource to protect:

1/ The Problem — Claude's context window fills fast. Every file read = tokens. Every command output = tokens. Every conversation turn = tokens. Full context = degraded performance.

2/ The Symptoms — Claude 'forgets' instructions, responses become confused, same mistakes repeated, quality drops noticeably. Context pollution is subtle. Then sudden.

3/ Strategy 1: /clear Between Tasks — Finished feature A? /clear. Start feature B. Fresh context = better performance. Don't let unrelated tasks accumulate.

4/ Strategy 2: Use Subagents for Exploration — 'Use a subagent to investigate the auth system.' Subagent explores in separate context. Reports back summary. Your context stays clean.

5/ Strategy 3: /compact When Needed — Need to preserve some context? '/compact Focus on the API changes.' Claude summarizes, keeps what matters, frees space.

6/ Strategy 4: Stop Correction Loops — Claude wrong → correct → still wrong → correct again. AFTER 2 CORRECTIONS: /clear. Write a better initial prompt. Fresh start > accumulated failures.

7/ The Rule of Thumb — One major task per session. Clear between unrelated tasks. Subagents for exploration. Stop correction loops early. Context management = productivity management.

Title: My automation broke for 3 days. Here's what I learned.
Body:
My automation broke for 3 days. Here's what I learned.

60 agents. All stopped. Zero errors in logs.

The silent failure that taught me the most.

THE SYMPTOM
Noticed on day 3: Nothing had run.
No GitHub syncs. No reports. No content.
But no errors either.

THE INVESTIGATION
Added verbose logging.
Traced execution path.
Found it: hardcoded path to a folder I'd moved.

Scheduler tried to access: /Users/old/path
Path didn't exist.
Error was caught and... swallowed.

THE LESSONS

1. Never hardcode paths
Use environment variables. Use relative paths. Paths change.

2. Fail loud, not quiet
That error handler that silently catches exceptions? It's hiding disasters. Make failures visible.

3. Health checks matter
Now every agent reports "I ran" to a central log. No report = something's wrong.

4. Redundancy in monitoring
Single point of failure in monitoring = you don't know when things fail.

THE RESULT
Silent failures are now impossible.
Every agent logs. Every failure alerts. Every path is dynamic.

Title: Your RAG system is probably broken

• Fixed-size chunks (breaks mid-thought)
• Pure vector search (misses exact matches)
• No source attribution (can't verify)
• Giant context windows (slow, expensive)

Most RAG tutorials teach these exact patterns.

WHAT ACTUALLY MATTERS

1. Chunking strategy
Don't split on character count. Use semantic boundaries.
Topic changes. Speaker transitions. Natural pauses.
SpaCy can detect these automatically.

2. Hybrid search
Vector search: "What's the concept?"
Keyword search: "Where's the exact term?"
Use both. My YouTubeRAG combines semantic + keyword.

3. Metadata preservation
Store source, timestamp, context with each chunk.
You'll need these for verification and navigation.

4. Test your retrieval
Before connecting to an LLM:
• Query the vector DB directly
• Check if right chunks return
• Measure precision/recall

Bad retrieval + good LLM = garbage output.

THE META-LESSON

RAG isn't about the model.
It's about the pipeline.

Fix chunking. Add hybrid search. Test retrieval.
Then worry about which LLM to use.

• Precise timing (9 AM daily)

Layer 3: Daily Scheduler
• Orchestrates agents
• Handles dependencies
• Logs everything

THE SETUP (macOS)

4. Load with launchctl

5 minutes of setup. Infinite reliability.

Mac restarts → automation resumes.
